nameStory: The name "capelin" comes from the French word "capelan," which fishermen used for these small, silvery fish that appeared in massive schools. The alternative spelling "caplin" is still commonly used in Newfoundland and maritime communities, reflecting the deep connection between these fish and coastal fishing traditions.
description: Atlantic capelin are small, slender fish from the smelt family that rarely venture into New England waters, preferring the colder northern Atlantic and Arctic oceans. These silvery fish grow to about 8-10 inches long, with olive-green backs that fade to bright silver sides. They're important "forage fish" that feed larger predators like cod, whales, and seabirds, spending most of their time in open ocean waters feeding on tiny plankton and krill.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and slender, reaching 8 inches for males and up to 10 inches for females - about the size of a large pencil

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Olive-green back that transitions to brilliant silver sides, creating a distinct two-toned appearance that catches light like polished metal

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined and torpedo-shaped with a slightly compressed body that feels firm and muscular when handled

idTips.label: Breeding Features
idTips.description: Males develop translucent ridges along both sides of their bodies and their bellies flash with reddish iridescence during spawning season

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in cold, open ocean waters rather than near shore - typically associated with Arctic and sub-Arctic conditions

habitat: Atlantic capelin are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, preferring the much colder waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. When they do appear in our region, it's typically in the deeper, colder offshore waters during unusual oceanographic conditions. They're most commonly found at the edge of ice shelves and in sub-Arctic waters where they can feed on dense plankton blooms.

seasonality.spring: Capelin migrate toward spawning areas, with some populations moving to sandy beaches while others spawn on offshore gravel beds.
seasonality.summer: Most active feeding period as they graze on dense plankton swarms in cold northern waters, rarely reaching New England during this time.
seasonality.fall: Post-spawning populations disperse to deeper waters, with males experiencing nearly 100% mortality after beach spawning events.
seasonality.winter: Remain in deep, cold offshore waters where they're least likely to be encountered in New England waters.

funFact: Male capelin have one of the most extreme breeding strategies in the fish world - when they spawn on beaches, nearly 100% of the males die immediately afterward, literally giving their lives for the next generation in a spectacular silvery sacrifice.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small smelt family members like rainbow smelt, but capelin have a more robust, torpedo-shaped body and lack the distinctive cucumber scent that fresh smelts have when handled.
contextualKnowledge: While capelin are incredibly important commercially and ecologically in northern waters like those around Newfoundland and Greenland, they're so rare in New England that most local anglers and naturalists will never encounter one - making any sighting quite special.
compareHints: As the only capelin species, compare capelin to their smelt family cousins like rainbow smelt. Capelin are more robust and torpedo-shaped compared to the more delicate, translucent appearance of rainbow smelt, and they lack the strong cucumber smell that characterizes fresh smelts. Capelin also have the distinctive translucent ridges on males that other smelts don't possess.
